title: The Road Not Taken: Counterfactual Conditionals
subtitle: Human beings spend a great deal of their lives in a world that never happened. English has a whole grammar for it — and it goes far beyond the third conditional.
intention: you'll work with the full range of unreal conditionals — mixed, inverted, elliptical and hedged — through the psychology of what might have been. By the end you should be able to build a counterfactual in four different shapes and choose between them.
warmup: Think of a moment when something nearly happened, or nearly didn't. How often do you still replay it?
Which hurts more, in your experience: something you did, or something you failed to do?
When someone says “at least it wasn't worse”, does that help you?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, work out the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: Psychologists use the word counterfactual for a thought about how events might have turned out differently.
items.meaning: counterfactual (noun/adj) — an imagined alternative to what actually happened: if only I had left ten minutes earlier.

items.sent: With hindsight, the warning signs were obvious; at the time, nobody saw them.
items.meaning: hindsight — understanding of an event only after it has happened. With the benefit of hindsight…

items.sent: She lost the race by two hundredths of a second — a near miss she has never quite got over.
items.meaning: near miss — an outcome that very nearly went the other way (also: an accident that almost happened).

items.sent: He dwells on the interview for weeks, going over every answer he gave.
items.meaning: dwell on — to keep thinking or talking about something unpleasant instead of moving on.

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: wistful · rumination · plausible. Read the meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (adjective) Seeming reasonable and likely to be true, though not proved.
items.meaning: plausible — “That's a plausible explanation, but the evidence is thin.”

items.sent: (noun) Repetitive thinking about the same distressing material, without reaching a conclusion.
items.meaning: rumination — “The line between reflection and rumination is where the thinking stops going anywhere.”

items.sent: (adjective) Quietly sad about something that is past or unattainable.
items.meaning: wistful — “She spoke about the year abroad in a wistful way.”

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: bitterly ___ it  ·  live to ___ it  ·  I have no ___s
items.meaning: regret (verb and noun) — sadness about something you did or failed to do.

items.sent: by a narrow ___  ·  a ___ of error  ·  win by a comfortable ___
items.meaning: margin — the amount by which something is won, lost or measured.

items.sent: a slim ___  ·  a ___ encounter  ·  stand a ___ of winning
items.meaning: chance — a possibility; also something happening by luck rather than plan.

vocab_use: Describe a decision you made by chance that turned out to matter.
Where is the line, for you, between useful reflection and rumination?
Is hindsight mostly a kindness or a curse?
story_heading: What might have been, in three studies

story.heading: Part 1 — The medal that makes people unhappy
paras: At the 1992 Olympic Games in Barcelona, three psychologists — Victoria Medvec, Scott Madey and Thomas Gilovich — recorded the faces of medal winners at the moment their events ended and again on the podium. They then showed the footage, with no sound and no context, to observers who knew nothing about who had won what, and asked them simply to rate how happy each athlete looked.

The result, published in 1995, was uncomfortable. The bronze medallists looked happier than the silver medallists who had beaten them. Objectively, silver is the better outcome; emotionally, it appeared to be the worse one.

The explanation the researchers offered is about comparison. The silver medallist's mind runs upwards: had I been a fraction faster, I would have won. The bronze medallist's runs downwards: had I been a fraction slower, I would have gone home with nothing. Each athlete is measured against a different imaginary result — and it is the imaginary result, not the real one, that seems to set the feeling. A conceptual replication published in 2020 found broadly the same pattern.
checks: What exactly did the observers see, and what were they asked to do?
Which imaginary outcome does each of the two medallists compare themselves with?
answers: Silent, context-free footage of medallists' faces; they rated how happy each athlete looked.
Bronze medallists appeared happier than silver medallists, although silver is objectively better.
Silver compares upwards with gold (“if I'd been slightly faster”); bronze compares downwards with fourth place (“if I'd been slightly slower, nothing”).
story.discuss: Where else do you see people made unhappy by an outcome that is objectively good?

story.heading: Part 2 — Two men at an airport
paras: Ten years earlier, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky had put a scenario to their readers. Mr Crane and Mr Tees leave for the airport in the same car, and are held up in the same traffic jam for the same thirty minutes. Both arrive thirty minutes after their scheduled departure times. Mr Crane's flight left on time. Mr Tees's flight was delayed, and left five minutes ago.
Almost everyone questioned said Mr Tees would be the more upset — although both men missed their flights by exactly the same margin of effort, and neither could have done anything differently.

Kahneman and Tversky's explanation was that our feelings follow how easily the mind can run the alternative film. Five minutes is easy to undo: had the lights been kinder, had he not stopped for coffee, and he would have been on that plane. Thirty minutes is not. They called this mental habit the simulation heuristic, and noticed that the mind prefers to undo the unusual: we rewrite the one day someone took a different route home, not the twenty years they took the usual one.
checks: In what way are the two men's situations identical?
Why do most people say Mr Tees is more upset?
What kind of detail does the mind prefer to undo?
answers: Same car, same traffic jam, same thirty-minute delay — both miss their flights.
Because the alternative is so easy to imagine: he missed it by only five minutes.
The unusual one — the day something was done differently, rather than the long-standing routine.
story.discuss: Think of a near miss in your own life. Which detail does your mind keep rewriting — and is it the one that actually mattered?

story.heading: Part 3 — What the alternative film is for
paras: Later researchers, notably Neal Roese and Kai Epstude, argued that counterfactual thinking is not a fault in the machine but a function of it. Upward counterfactuals — how it could have gone better — are largely preparative: they extract a lesson for next time. Downward ones — how it could have gone worse — are largely affective: they comfort. The trouble begins when the upward ones will not switch off, a pattern associated with anxiety and low mood.

There is also a curious pattern in what people regret. Gilovich and Medvec reported that in the short term we regret our actions — the thing we said, the money we spent — while over a lifetime we regret our inactions more: the course not taken, the letter never sent, the person never asked. The sting of a bad decision fades; the wondering does not.

The same grammar can be turned round and pointed forwards. The psychologist Gary Klein proposed a technique he called the pre-mortem: before a project begins, the team is told to imagine that a year has passed and the project has failed completely — and then to explain why. Teams that would never have raised an objection out loud will happily describe a disaster that has already, in the imagination, occurred.
checks: What are upward and downward counterfactuals for, according to Roese and Epstude?
How does regret change over time?
What does a pre-mortem ask a team to do?
answers: Upward ones prepare us for next time; downward ones comfort us.
In the short term we regret what we did; over a lifetime we regret what we didn't do.
Imagine the project has already failed a year from now, and explain why.
story.discuss: Why might it be easier to criticise a plan that has “already failed” than one that is only being proposed?

grammar.name: Counterfactuals in Depth
grammar.lead: Every sentence in that story lives in an unreal world, and English marks that world by moving the tense one step back. Below is the full range — not a ladder of first, second and third, but a set of choices about distance, direction in time and register.
notes:
1 · Mixed conditionals — the two directions. The two halves of a conditional can sit in different times.
Past condition → present result: “If she had taken that job in Lisbon, she would be fluent by now.”
Present condition → past result: “If he weren't so proud, he would have asked for help.”
Choose by asking: when is the condition, and when is the result?

2 · Inversion — the formal, literary register. Drop if and put the auxiliary first.
“Had the flight not been delayed, he would never have reached the gate.”
“Were the decision mine, I would postpone it.”  “Were he to resign, the whole board would follow.”
“Should you change your mind, the offer stands.” (= if you happen to)
Negatives are not contracted: “Had it not been for the rain…” — never ~~Hadn't it been~~.

3 · But for, were it not for, otherwise. Compressed conditions.
“But for a single dropped catch, England would have won.” (= if it had not been for)
“Were it not for the traffic, we'd be there.”  “I had a map. Otherwise I'd still be walking.”

4 · The unreal past after other triggers. The same backshift appears without if:
suppose / supposing / what if / imagine + past (or past perfect): “Suppose you had said nothing — what then?”
if only / I wish: “If only he had asked.”  I'd rather / I'd sooner + past: “I'd rather you didn't.”
it's (high) time + past: “It's high time we left.”  as if / as though + past: “He talks about it as though it were yesterday.”

5 · Degrees of distance. Compare: “If the price rises…” (a live possibility) · “If the price were to rise…” (deliberately remote, hypothetical) · “If the price should rise…” (unlikely, but let's plan) · “If the price happens to rise…” (chance).
This is how careful speakers hold an idea at arm's length without denying it.

6 · The traps. ~~If I would have known~~ → “If I had known”.  ~~Had I have known~~ → “Had I known”.  ~~I wish I would have gone~~ → “I wish I had gone”.  ~~unless he doesn't come~~ → “unless he comes”.  Were, not was, in the formal unreal: “If I were you”, “Were she here…”.

exercises.heading: Rewrite without if
exercises.intro: Express the same condition using inversion, but for or otherwise, as indicated. Write the full clause.
items: 1. If the referee had seen it, the goal would have been disallowed. (inversion) → ___ , the goal would have been disallowed.
2. If it had not been for her evidence, the case would have collapsed. (but for) → ___ , the case would have collapsed.
3. If you should need any further information, please contact us. (inversion) → ___ , please contact us.
4. If the government were to raise the tax, imports would fall. (inversion) → ___ , imports would fall.
5. We took the earlier train. If we hadn't, we would have missed the opening. (otherwise) → We took the earlier train; ___ .
answers: 1. Had the referee seen it
2. But for her evidence
3. Should you need any further information
4. Were the government to raise the tax
5. otherwise we would have missed the opening

exercises.heading: Mixed conditionals: which direction?
exercises.intro: Read the situation and complete the conditional. Decide first when the condition is, and when the result is.
items: 1. He didn't study medicine, and today he works in insurance. → If he ___ (study) medicine, he ___ (work) in insurance today.
2. She is a nervous flyer, so she refused the job in Singapore last year. → If she ___ (not be) a nervous flyer, she ___ (accept) the job.
3. They sold the flat in 2019. Prices have doubled since. → Had they ___ (keep) the flat, they ___ (be) considerably better off now.
4. I don't speak Japanese, so I didn't understand the announcement. → If I ___ (speak) Japanese, I ___ (understand) the announcement.
5. He missed the deadline, and he is not on the shortlist. → Were it not for that missed deadline, he ___ (be) on the shortlist now.
answers: 1. had studied … wouldn't be working (past condition → present result)
2. weren't … would have accepted (present condition → past result)
3. kept … would be
4. spoke … would have understood
5. would be

exercises.heading: Find and fix
exercises.intro: Each sentence contains one error — and each error is a common one. Write the correction.
items: 1. If I would have known you were coming, I'd have waited. → ___
2. Had I have realised how late it was, I'd have called. → ___
3. I wish I would have taken that job when it was offered. → ___
4. Hadn't it been for the rain, the match would have finished. → ___
5. It's high time we discuss this properly. → ___
6. He describes the accident as if it was happening now. → ___
answers: 1. If I had known… (never would have in the if-clause)
2. Had I realised… (inversion doesn't take an extra have)
3. I wish I had taken…
4. Had it not been for the rain… (no contraction in inversion)
5. It's high time we discussed this properly.
6. …as if it were happening now. (the careful form; was is common in speech)

grammar.closing: Now say three sentences about your own last twelve months: one mixed conditional, one inverted, and one with but for.

deeper.heading: Going deeper — the same grammar, different work
deeper.lead: Counterfactuals do not only describe; they assign blame, offer comfort, soften a claim and test an idea. The structure barely changes. What changes is what the speaker is doing with it.

blocks.heading: Where the blame lands
paras: Every counterfactual chooses something to undo, and the thing you choose to undo is the thing you quietly hold responsible. Notice how much moves between these two sentences, though the grammar is identical.

pairs.a: “If you hadn't left so late, you'd have caught it.”
pairs.b: The undone element is a person's choice — so the sentence allocates fault, whatever the speaker intended.

pairs.a: “If the train hadn't been cancelled, you'd have caught it.”
pairs.b: The undone element is circumstance. The same event, the same structure, no blame.

blocks.heading: Comfort, and how it fails
paras: “At least…” is a downward counterfactual offered to someone else. It can land as kindness or as dismissal, and the difference is mostly about whether the other person has finished describing the loss.
Compare the effect of “At least it was quick” with “I keep thinking how it might have gone otherwise” — the second stays inside the other person's version of events instead of replacing it.

blocks.heading: Distance as tact
paras: The further back you shift the tense, the less committed you sound — which is why the unreal forms do so much diplomatic work. Rewrite each blunt line as something tentative, using the structure in brackets. Say it aloud before you reveal.

items.q: You should have told me earlier. (had + inversion, no blame)
items.a: “Had I known earlier, I could have done something about it.” — the sentence now undoes my ignorance rather than your silence.
“Were we to go ahead as planned, I think we'd run into trouble with the timing.”

items.q: Stop talking about it. (I'd rather + past)
items.a: “I'd rather we left that for another day.”

items.q: Tell me what you'd do if you lost the contract. (suppose + past)
items.a: “Suppose the contract went elsewhere — what would the next six months look like?”

items.q: This proposal will fail. (pre-mortem: imagine + present perfect / past)
items.a: “Imagine it's a year from now and this has failed completely. What went wrong?”

discuss: Is there a way to say “if only you had…” to someone that genuinely helps? What would have to be true about the moment?
Some languages mark the unreal much more lightly than English. Does a heavier grammar make the thinking heavier too?
The pre-mortem asks people to describe a failure that hasn't happened. Why does that produce honesty that a normal meeting doesn't?

speak.intro: Now use the structures on your own material. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk. Aim to use at least one inverted conditional and one mixed conditional in each answer.
speak.useful: “Had I …, I would have …” · “If I hadn't …, I wouldn't be … now” · “But for …” · “Were it not for …” · “Suppose it had gone the other way …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — The near miss
paras: Describe something that very nearly went differently. What is the “if only” sentence — and has it changed over the years?

tasks.label: Task 2 — Action or inaction
paras: Think of one thing you did and one thing you didn't do. Which one do you still think about, and why that one?

tasks.label: Task 3 — The pre-mortem
paras: Take a plan you have now. Imagine it is a year later and it has failed completely. Explain what went wrong.

tasks.label: Task 4 — The comfort test
paras: Someone tells you “at least it wasn't worse”. Say when that comforts you, and when it irritates you.

final: If regret over inaction grows with time, what follows for how a person should make decisions at thirty? At sixty?
Counterfactual thinking is what makes both learning and rumination possible. Can you have the first without risking the second?
Should children be taught to run alternative versions of events — or protected from it?
From memory: retell the airport story in four sentences, using an inverted conditional, a mixed conditional, but for, and as though.
